name: Arch of Marcus Aurelius
summary: The best-preserved Roman monument of ancient Oea, a four-faced marble triumphal arch at the edge of the Old City.
history: Built in 165 AD by Gaius Calpurnius Celsus, a magistrate of Oea, to mark Lucius Verus's victories over the Parthians (161-66). It is a four-faced marble arch with an unusual octagonal dome; Apollo and Minerva, the city's patron gods, appear on the pediments. It was partly buried over the centuries. Statues of the emperor and Verus were recovered in 19th-century digs, and the four niches are now empty. The Italian administration did conservation work in 1914-1918, and the architect Florestano Di Fausto reorganised the surroundings in the 1930s. It was only slightly damaged in World War II.
today: As of 2017 it suffered from poor upkeep, visitor damage and acid rain wearing away its carved detail.
uncertain: Wikipedia gives 165 AD and says it was built at Oea. A travel-site page (Temehu) says 163 AD and that it was moved from Leptis Magna; that claim is not supported elsewhere in the sources opened. Nothing was found on its Gaddafi-era treatment. Coordinates are from OpenStreetMap.

name: Red Castle (Assaraya al-Hamra) and National Museum
summary: The great waterfront fortress and palace beside Martyrs' Square, in use for centuries as the seat of rulers and since 1919 as Libya's national museum.
history: Its origins are unclear; some accounts reach back to Oea. The Spanish took the city in 1510, and the Knights of St John held it from 1530 to 1551; much of the present structure dates from the Knights' period. After 1551 Ottoman governors lived there, and from 1711 it was the seat of the Karamanli pashas. The Italians made it the governor's headquarters after 1911 and opened Libya's first museum in part of it in 1919. Armando Brasini remodelled it in 1922-23, and a Mussolini equestrian statue stood before it from 1938. The British used it from 1942-43, and an expanded museum reopened in 1948. Its entrance faces Martyrs' Square.
era: In the 1970s the seafront highway cut the castle off from the sea and left Saraya Lake. The government refurbished the museum from 1982 to 1988, and it opened to the public in 1988 as the Assaraya Alhamra Museum. Items belonging to Gaddafi, including a coloured Volkswagen Beetle, were displayed there, and rebels in 2011 damaged a few of them.
today: The museum closed after 2011 and again in 2015. Wikipedia reports it reopened on 12 December 2025 as the National Museum of Libya, at first for school groups only. The Department of Archaeology is also based there.
uncertain: Who first built the castle is not settled. Sources disagree on when it reopened after 2015 and on details of the Knights' dates (1528 vs 1530). Whether it served as a prison is not documented in the pages opened.

sources.t: OpenStreetMap way 100827834 (The Red Castle) (project extract landmarks.json)

name: Old City (Medina) of Tripoli and its walls
summary: The walled historic core on the harbour, shaped by Phoenician, Roman, Spanish, Knights, Ottoman, Karamanli and Italian layers.
history: Phoenicians founded the city in the 7th century BC and the Romans called it Oea. The Spanish took it in 1510, the Knights of St John held it from 1530, and the Ottomans captured it in 1551. The Ottoman governor Dragut repaired the walls, giving the old city its roughly pentagonal shape. Most surviving mosques, baths, souqs and consulates date from the Ottoman and Karamanli periods (1551-1835). Italians built new squares and avenues beside it from 1911. Its chief gates include Bab al-Bahr on the harbour side and a main entrance often called Bab al-Hurriya (Freedom Gate).
today: OpenStreetMap shows a Historic Cities Administration office inside it. No recent survey of its condition was found.
uncertain: The full circuit of the walls today, and which gates survive, was not established from the sources opened. Whether Bab al-Hurriya is the same as the gate called Bab Jedid or Bab Zanata is not stated.

name: Bab Darghouth (Dragut Gate)
summary: A gate of the Old City near the Dragut Mosque, named with the Arabic form of the Ottoman commander's name.
history: OpenStreetMap records a city gate named Bab Darghouth in the Old City, close to the Dragut (Darghut) Mosque and the Othman Pasha madrasa. An old-city walking account says the alley beside the mosque is the way into the medina. Darghouth is the Arabic form of Dragut, the Ottoman governor who took Tripoli in 1551 and repaired its walls. The date and builder of this particular gate were not found in the sources opened.
today: A gate point is mapped in OpenStreetMap; its present condition is not documented here.
uncertain: Date, builder and exact relation to the surviving walls are unknown. The name link to Dragut is an inference from the spelling.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: Othman Pasha School in Tripoli

name: Bab al-Bahr (Sea Gate)
summary: The harbour-side gate of the Old City, giving its name to the quarter around the Dragut and Gurgi mosques.
history: Bab al-Bahr opens from the old city toward the harbour. Dragut, killed at Malta in 1565, was buried in the nearby Sidi Darghut Mosque, close to this gate. The Gurgi Mosque (1834) is in the Bab al-Bahr district near the sea, and the Othman Pasha madrasa (1654) lies on the central axis running from the seafront into the city. The date of the gate itself, and any Italian-era changes, were not found in the sources opened.
today: Visitors reach the medina from here; its present state is not documented in the sources opened.
uncertain: No coordinates were seen on a page I opened, and the gate does not appear in the OpenStreetMap extract, so none are given. Gate date is unknown.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: Othman Pasha School in Tripoli

name: Bab Jedid (New Gate) and Bab Zanata
summary: A western gate of the Old City opened in the 1860s to replace the earlier Bab Zanata.
history: Bab Zanata was blocked during the civil war of 1831 under Ali II Karamanli. An inscription dated 12 February 1865 says residents asked the Ottoman governor to open a new gate in its place, and it became known as Bab Jedid, the New Gate. Wikipedia's timeline dates the opening of Bab el-Jedid to 1860, so sources differ on the year. The gate sits on the western side of the old city.
today: One of the main gates of the medina according to the page opened; present condition not documented.
uncertain: Year (1860 vs 1865) differs between sources. It is not stated whether Bab al-Hurriya (Freedom Gate) is the same as Bab Jedid. No coordinates were found.

sources.t: Alive in Libya: Al-Madina gates and alleys

name: Dragut (Sidi Darghut) Mosque and tomb
summary: The first Ottoman-style mosque in Tripoli, built after the 1551 conquest and holding the tomb of the commander Dragut.
history: Built around 1560 on the site of a Hospitaller church, which local tradition says was kept inside the mosque. Dragut died at the 1565 Siege of Malta and was buried here with his family. Iskander Pasha altered it in the early 1600s and rebuilt the minaret in 1602. Monument surveyors visited in 1921 and it was restored in the 1920s. Bombing in World War II badly damaged the central part. Ali Mohamed Abu Zaian led the rebuilding, which differs from the original; the domes rose from 27 to 32. One account dates the restoration to 1946.
today: Still a mosque; in 2014 armed men tried several times to vandalise it and were repelled.
uncertain: Sources give the construction year as 1556, about 1560 or 1565. Nothing was found on the Gaddafi period. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.

sources.t: Alive in Libya: Al-Madina gates and alleys

name: Hammam Dragut (Darghouth Turkish Bath)
summary: An Ottoman bath attached to the Dragut Mosque and tomb in the Old City.
history: The bath is annexed to the Sidi Darghut Mosque and tomb. Wikipedia dates it to 1081 AH (1670-71). Its timeline separately lists an Iskandar Pasha hammam built in 1604, and the mosque page says Iskander Pasha built or renovated a bath in the early 1600s. The old-city map from a travel site names three hammams: Hammam Darghut, Hammam al-Kebira and Hammam Alheygha. A Manchester research record also covers the surviving historic hammams of the medina.
today: Present use is not stated in the sources opened.
uncertain: Whether the 1604 Iskandar Pasha bath and the 1670-71 Darghouth bath are the same building is unclear. No coordinates were found.

name: Gurgi Mosque
summary: A late Karamanli-era mosque near the harbour, built by a naval captain from Georgia and housing his family tomb.
history: Completed in 1834 for Mustafa Gurgi, a naval captain whose name means "from Georgia". It was built in the last years of Karamanli rule, after Pasha Yusuf Karamanli (reigned 1795-1832). It stands in the Bab al-Bahr district of the old city, near the sea, as part of a complex with a tomb and a school. The tomb of Gurgi and his family is in the antechamber. The Ottomans resumed direct control of Tripoli the following year, in 1835.
today: An active Sunni mosque and a tourist attraction. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.
uncertain: Nothing was found on its Gaddafi-era use or any restoration.

name: Ahmed Pasha Karamanli Mosque
summary: The mosque, madrasa and dynastic mausoleum founded by Ahmed Karamanli, near the clock tower and Souq al-Mushir.
history: Ahmed Karamanli, founder of the dynasty that ruled from 1711, began the mosque in 1736. Another source gives 1736-1738. It has 25 domes, a madrasa and a mausoleum for members of the family. It stands beside Souq al-Mushir, next to the Red Castle, and a 1994 photograph shows it framed with the clock tower through a souq gate. The Karamanlis ruled Tripolitania until the Ottomans removed them in 1835.
today: In 2014, during fighting in Libya, the mosque was vandalised and its ceramic tiles and marble decoration were damaged; UNESCO condemned the attack.
uncertain: No coordinates were seen on any page opened. Completion date and any Italian or Gaddafi-era restoration were not found.

sources.t: MIT Dome: suq gate toward Qaramanli mosque and clock tower

name: Naqa (Al-Naqah) Mosque
summary: Probably the oldest Islamic monument in Tripoli, rebuilt in 1610-11 and reusing Roman and Byzantine columns.
history: Its early history is poorly documented. It was most likely first built in 973 under the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz. Two legends explain the name "Mosque of the Camel", both involving a gold-laden camel. It was badly damaged or destroyed during the Spanish occupation in the 16th century. An inscription records rebuilding in 1610-11 by the Ottoman-era governor Safar Dey. The prayer hall has 36 columns, including reused Roman and Byzantine ones, and 42 domes. The floor now lies about 0.4 m below street level.
today: An active mosque. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.
uncertain: The 973 date is a probable one only. Nothing on Gaddafi-era use or recent restoration was found.

name: Sidi Salem Mosque
summary: An old mosque of the medina that predates the Spanish conquest and was restored in the Ottoman period.
history: Wikipedia dates Sidi Salem to the late 15th century with a restoration in 1670. That places it before the Spanish conquest of 1510, the Knights' rule from 1530 and the Ottoman capture of 1551. Its timeline repeats the 1670 restoration. It is one of the older religious buildings of the old city alongside the Naqa Mosque. No founder or architectural description was found in the pages opened.
uncertain: Location within the medina, founder and later history are not documented in the sources opened. No coordinates are given.

name: Uthman Pasha Madrasa
summary: A 17th-century Quranic school beside the Dragut Mosque that still teaches.
history: Founded in 1654 under Ottoman rule and named for the governor Othman Pasha al-Saqizli. It lies in the Bab al-Bahr area near the Dragut entrance, on the axis leading from the sea into the city. A square courtyard leads to more than ten marble rooms under two Ottoman domes, and a courtyard shows inscriptions and Ottoman taps. Mohammed Kamel Ben Mustafa, born in 1828 in Zawiya, studied and taught there.
today: Still operating as a religious school with study circles, according to a 2020s article.
uncertain: Whether Othman Pasha personally paid for it is not stated. No coordinates were found.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: Othman Pasha School in Tripoli

name: Ottoman Clock Tower
summary: An 18 m Ottoman clock tower rising over the small square at the head of Souq al-Mushir.
history: The Ottoman governor had it built between 1866 and 1870; Wikipedia's timeline gives 1870 and a photograph archive says "mid-19th century". It stands about 18 metres tall in Al-Sa'aa (Clock) Square, near the end of Souq al-Mushir, the Karamanli Mosque and the Red Castle. The square is also home to the brassware market.
today: Still a city landmark. The point shown is the mapped Clock Square (Meydan Assa'a) in OpenStreetMap, not the tower's own point.
uncertain: Exact year (1866-70) and the Ottoman official who ordered it are not named in the sources opened. Nothing found on its Gaddafi-era condition.

sources.t: MIT Dome (Aga Khan Visual Archive): Ottoman Clock Tower

name: Turkish (Ottoman) Prison
summary: A building in the Old City labelled the Turkish Prison on maps, near the Marcus Aurelius Arch.
history: A Turkish Prison appears on an old-city map from a travel site, with the label "(O. Church)", which may mean it occupied a former church. OpenStreetMap places an attraction called The Turkish Prison just south of the Marcus Aurelius Arch. In the Ottoman period (1551-1911) the Red Castle also served as the governors' stronghold. No dates, builder or inmate records were found in the sources opened.
today: Present state not documented.
uncertain: The map label and the OpenStreetMap point are the only documentation. Whether it was a prison under the Karamanlis, the Ottomans or both, and when it closed, are unknown.

sources.t: OpenStreetMap node 12318353501 (The Turkish Prison) (project extract landmarks.json)

name: Souq al-Mushir
summary: An open-air market street named for the Ottoman governor Rajab Pasha, running from the Huwara souq toward the clock tower.
history: Built by the Ottoman governor Rajab Pasha, who ruled Tripoli in 1906-1908, and named for his title al-Mushir. It runs from the opening of Souq al-Huwara on the south-east toward the clock tower. It originally sold flowers, medicinal herbs and gardening supplies. The Karamanli Mosque stands on it. A timeline gives 1935 for the souq's reconstruction under the Italians.
today: Now sells clothes, household goods, food and hardware.
uncertain: The Italian reconstruction of 1935 is listed only in one timeline. OpenStreetMap maps a gate called Bab al-Mushir near the Red Castle, but the souq itself has no coordinates here.

name: Souq al-Turk
summary: One of the longest markets of the Old City, a covered and open street that became a showcase for fine textiles and jewellery.
history: Created by an Ottoman governor and named for its resemblance to open markets in Turkey. It lies in two connected parts, one covered opposite the clock tower and one open. Under the Italians its character shifted from oriental to western European, and it was crowded on Sundays. Traders were mostly Jewish, with some Italians, Indians and Africans. Jewish families ran toy and sewing shops there. Nearby Souq al-Hrara sold silk and was also mostly Jewish-run.
uncertain: Which governor founded it and when is not clear; the source names a "Wali Mohamed Bahsa" with a doubtful spelling. Souq al-Rabaa was not found in sources opened. No coordinates.

name: Old British Consulate (Karamanli-era house)
summary: A decorated courtyard house built by the Karamanli family in 1744 and once the residence of the British consul.
history: Built by the Karamanli family in 1744 and used as the residence of the British Consul. A small doorway off Shar'a al-Kuwash opens onto a large decorated courtyard, according to Philip Ward's 1969 guidebook as summarised by Archnet. Other foreign consulates also operated in the city; Wikipedia's Karamanli page names only the US consulate, whose flagpole Yusuf Karamanli had cut down in May 1801. The old-city map from a travel site also lists an Old French Consulate.
today: Mapped in OpenStreetMap as "Old British Consulate"; its present use is not documented.
uncertain: The 1744 date and the house's use come from a single guidebook summary. Whether the OpenStreetMap point matches that exact house is unconfirmed. Locations of other consulates (US, French) were not found.

sources.t: OpenStreetMap node 13022191845 (Old British Consulate) (project extract landmarks.json)

name: Karamanli House Museum (Harem of Ali Karamanli)
summary: A two-storey 18th-century Karamanli house in the Old City, now a small museum of domestic life.
history: Built in the second half of the 18th century during the reign of Ali Pasha Karamanli (1754-1793). It was first known as the Harem House, and Yusuf Pasha is said to have lived there until his death. In the second Ottoman period (after 1835) a consulate, called "Tuscania" on the source page, was based in it. The two-storey house has a fountain and mosaic-covered walls, four rooms and a kitchen downstairs, and costumes, furniture and a weapons room above.
era: The Old City Project restored it in the early 1990s and it was officially opened on 27 October 1994 as the "Tripoli Historical Exhibition". It displays furniture, copper and brass, clothing, jewellery and early gadgets such as a gramophone, a telephone and a radio.
today: Operating status is not confirmed; the page quoting entrance fees may be out of date.
uncertain: The page gives two slightly different restoration dates. The OpenStreetMap point is labelled "The Harem of Ali Garamanli". Whether "Tuscania" is a correct consulate name is unclear.

sources.t: OpenStreetMap node 12318285901 (The Harem of Ali Garamanli) (project extract landmarks.json)

name: Church of Santa Maria degli Angeli (Our Lady of the Angels)
summary: The oldest surviving Catholic church of Tripoli, in a small square of the Old City, later handed to Anglicans.
history: Wikipedia's timeline lists the church as built in 1846, and the cathedral page says it was the first Catholic church consecrated in Tripoli (1870). An old-city article instead says it was built by Italian Capuchin monks in the 17th century. A Greek Orthodox church, St George, stands in the same square. Colonial-era Italian photographs show it among the buildings of the old city.
era: According to the old-city article, Colonel Gaddafi gave the church to the Anglican faith, and it holds Anglican services. Gaddafi confiscated Italian and church property in July 1970 and closed the Italian cathedral in September 1970.
today: Reported as in Anglican use.
uncertain: Dates conflict (17th century, 1846, 1870). The coordinates are those of the OpenStreetMap area labelled "Santa Maria Square", which is the likeliest square but is not confirmed as the church site.

sources.t: Alive in Libya: Al-Madina gates and alleys
OpenStreetMap way 870738622 (Santa Maria Square) (project extract landmarks.json)

name: Dar Bishi Synagogue
summary: A synagogue in the old Jewish Quarter that was the focus of a short-lived reopening in 2011.
history: Dar Bishi stood in the Hara Kebira, the old Jewish Quarter of the medina. Tripoli had about 14,000 Jews in 1903, and in 1941 Jews were about a quarter of the city, with 44 synagogues. Rioters in November 1945 looted nearly all the city's synagogues and destroyed five. Italy's racial laws from 1938 removed Jews from public office and state schools. Most Jews left after 1948 and 1967.
era: After 1969 Jewish property was confiscated and fewer than 40 Jews remained by 1972. Diarna says the last member of the Jewish community died in 2003 (another source says the last Jew was allowed to leave that year). In 2011 David Gerbi began clearing the building and reopened it for prayer, but work stopped on 8 October 2011 after protests.
today: Condition and ownership unknown; Diarna made a 3D digital reconstruction.
uncertain: Foundation date and its exact street are not given in sources opened. Wikipedia says Gerbi removed a brick wall blocking the entrance. Later reports of conversion or demolition were not verified, so no coordinates are given.

sources.t: Wikipedia: History of the Jews in Libya

name: Hara Kebira (Jewish Quarter)
summary: The historic Jewish quarter inside the Old City, where Dar Bishi and many other synagogues stood.
history: Hara Kebira ("great quarter") was the main Jewish neighbourhood of the Old City. Jews ran many shops in nearby Souq al-Turk and Souq al-Hrara in the Italian period. The Alliance Israélite counted about 14,000 Jews in Tripoli in 1903; in 1941 they were 25 percent of the population with 44 synagogues. The 1945 riots (5-7 November) left about 4,000 Jews homeless. Violence in June 1948 killed 12 more, and after the 1967 war over 6,000 were evacuated to Rome.
era: After the 1969 coup Jewish property was confiscated and debts owed to Jews were cancelled. Jewish men were arrested, and fewer than 40 Jews remained by 1972. One account says the last Jew, an elderly woman, was allowed to leave in 2003.
uncertain: Exact boundaries of the quarter were not documented in the sources opened. Its present occupants and condition are unknown.

sources.t: Wikipedia: History of the Jews in Libya

name: Jewish Cemetery of Tripoli
summary: The main Jewish burial ground of Tripoli, on the coast west of the city, largely built over after 1969.
history: A 1943 photograph shows Allied soldiers surveying the cemetery after the Germans had used many of its gravestones for coastal defences as the Eighth Army advanced. It lay on the coast just west of Tripoli. OpenStreetMap maps an "Old Jews Graveyard" next to the Italian cemetery and Tripoli War Cemetery in the Hammangi area. Libya's Jewish population fell from about 40,000 in World War II to about 100 by 1969.
era: In 2002 David Gerbi found children playing among debris with human remains. By 2007 he found the debris cleared, a highway built over the site and a high-rise on it. An Israeli news interview with Meir Kachlon claims Gaddafi crushed the graves and dumped them in the sea, and that the area was built over. These accounts are not independently verified.
today: A virtual cemetery project was announced to replace the destroyed Jewish cemeteries.
uncertain: How the OpenStreetMap graveyard relates to the larger cemetery described in news reports is unknown. Kachlon gives 130 acres, unconfirmed. When it was destroyed is not dated. Founding date unknown.

sources.t: Times of Israel: Libya's Jewish graveyards were destroyed
Jewish Refugees: Gaddafi bulldozed Jewish cemetery into the sea
OpenStreetMap way 100872906 (Old Jews Graveyard) (project extract landmarks.json)

name: Italian Cathedral (Algeria Square / Gamal Abdel Nasser Mosque)
summary: Tripoli's Italian Romanesque Revival cathedral, now a mosque on Algeria Square.
history: Construction began about 1923, with the foundation stone laid that January. It opened in 1928, was consecrated on 24-26 November 1928, and the 60 m bell tower was completed in December 1931. Saffo Panteri designed the basilica with a dome 46 m high. It served a settler population of about 25,000 and was the second Catholic church consecrated in Tripoli, after Santa Maria degli Angeli. A Eucharistic Congress was held in Tripoli on 24 November 1937. A Libyan blog credits Governor De Bono with completing it.
era: In July 1970 the Revolutionary Council confiscated Italian and church property. In September 1970 the Vicar Apostolic of Benghazi was expelled and the cathedral was closed. It became a mosque (Gamal Abdel Nasser Mosque, also Algeria Square Mosque) and the square was renamed Algeria Square. The conversion date is uncertain; the exterior changes were fully visible by about 1998-2000.
today: Open to the public as a mosque. The overall shape and bell tower remain, but the facade and interior were heavily altered. St Francis pro-cathedral is the temporary Catholic cathedral.
uncertain: Exact conversion date. Coordinates from the Wikipedia infobox (32°53'26"N 13°11'9"E).

name: Piazza Italia / Independence Square / Green Square / Martyrs' Square
summary: The central square beside the Red Castle that has changed names with each regime.
history: The Italians built it on the site of the old bread market (souq al-khubs) and expanded it several times in the 1930s; Florestano Di Fausto designed the square around the castle. After independence in 1951 it was called Independence Square. Streets meeting there include Omar Mukhtar Avenue, Independence Street (leading to King Idris's palace), 24 December Avenue and Mizran Street. A large fountain designed by an Italian architect stood at its centre, and a seafront avenue is marked by two tall pillars.
era: After 1969 it was renamed Green Square after the Green Book. The Royal Miramare Theatre, opposite the Red Castle, was demolished by his government after the 1960s to make room for mass rallies. Protests took place there on 20 and 25 March 2011.
today: Rebels took it on 21-22 August 2011 and renamed it Martyrs' Square; crowds celebrated there on 31 August and 2 September.
uncertain: No coordinates were seen on any page opened. It lies directly in front of the Red Castle entrance, but no exact centre is given.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: Tripoli's lost elegance of Miramare Theatre

name: Uaddan Hotel and Casino (Al Waddan Hotel)
summary: A glamorous Italian-era seafront hotel with a casino and theatre, later restored as a luxury hotel.
history: Built in 1935 (opened 1936) as the Italian Uaddan Hotel and Casino, alongside the Hotel Al Mehari. The architect was Florestano Di Fausto, working with Stefano Gatti-Casazza. It had a casino and a 500-seat theatre. An American journalist called it "the Waldorf Astoria of Tripoli" and it has been described as a jewel of modern African architecture. Wikipedia places the Grand Hotel just to its west.
today: Fully restored between 2007 and 2009 at about $16 million as an international luxury hotel, managed for several years by InterContinental. Coordinates from the Wikipedia infobox.
uncertain: The infobox says 1935 and the text says 1936 for the opening. Current operating status after 2011 was not found.

name: Grand Hotel of Tripoli (Italian original)
summary: A large Italian-era seafront hotel of 350 rooms near the cathedral, later demolished and replaced.
history: Designed by Florestano Di Fausto in 1920 according to a Libyan blog, though Wikipedia's timeline lists the Grand Hotel under 1925 and says it may date from 1924. It stood in an open park overlooking the port near what is now the Algerian Embassy and the Gamal Abdel Nasser (former cathedral) Mosque. The hotel had 350 rooms and was known for its many arches. It sits next to the Al Waddan Hotel.
era: The blog says the original was demolished in the 1980s and a new hotel on the same site was designed by a British company in 1982. The exterior wall of the new building shows a picture of the original.
today: The new hotel was deserted after 2011 according to the blog.
uncertain: Design year (1920) and opening year (1924/1925) differ; the demolition date and the 1982 rebuilding come from one blog citing a Facebook group. Corinthia Hotel Tripoli (2003) is a different building. No coordinates found.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: The Grand Hotel of Tripoli

name: Royal Palace of Tripoli (Qasr al-Khuld) / Italian Governor's Palace
summary: A large palace built for the Italian governors of Tripolitania, later the monarch's Tripoli residence, then a public library.
history: Built in 1924-1931 during Italian rule to a design by Saul Meraviglia Mantegazza, as the residence of the colonial governors of Italian Tripolitania. A Libyan blog says Governor De Bono, in office from 1925, completed the Governor's Palace; Wikipedia's timeline gives 1929. It later became the residence of the Libyan monarch in Tripoli. A palace-secretary memoir says the Tripoli palace hosted routine visits and that the royal palaces were modest villas. Independence Street leads from Independence Square to King Idris's palace.
era: After Colonel Gaddafi's 1969 coup the palace was converted into a public library, ending its use as a royal residence. The Wikipedia page gives no further detail on its use during the Gaddafi period or on any changes to the building.
today: What the building is used for now was not stated. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.
uncertain: Which monarch lived there is not stated. A Royal Palace "in Gargaresh" and a separate "Government Palace" were not found in any source; it may be the same building. A Libyan Museum building appears near these coordinates in OpenStreetMap but was not matched.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: Queen Fatima's private secretary, 1968-69

name: Banco di Roma and Banco di Napoli buildings
summary: Branches of the first Italian banks in Tripoli, plus the Bank of Italy headquarters of the 1920s.
history: Banco di Roma was the first Italian bank in Tripoli, opening in 1907. Banco di Napoli received authority for a Tripoli branch in December 1911, and its Tripoli building stood on Corso Vittorio Emanuele; its sources date the opening to 1913 or to an inauguration on 30 November 1930. The Bank of Italy building went up in the 1920s under governor De Bono. The Banco di Roma building is also marked on a tourist map of the old city, and directions to the Othman Pasha madrasa say to walk toward the Banco di Roma from Bab al-Bahr.
era: On 13 November 1969 the Libyan government nationalised Banco di Napoli and turned it into a Libyan joint-stock company. Its Tripoli operations had resumed fully in 1952 after British oversight began in 1946. The Italian community was expelled in 1970.
uncertain: Exact addresses and architects are not given in the sources opened. Which present building is the Banco di Roma is unconfirmed, so no coordinates. Banco di Napoli operations resumed in 1952 after British oversight in 1946.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: Othman Pasha School in Tripoli

name: Royal Miramare Theatre
summary: The largest theatre in Tripoli, a 2,000-seat Italian opera house opposite the Red Castle, now demolished.
history: Opened in 1925 as the Real Teatro Miramare during the governorship of Emilio De Bono; Wikipedia's timeline lists it with 1928 buildings. It seated 2,000 and staged operas, including Verdi's Un ballo in maschera, and hosted Italian and European companies. It stood opposite the Corniche, across from the Red Castle. Allied bombing in World War II heavily damaged it, and it was still maintained until independence.
era: Wikipedia says Gaddafi's government demolished it after the 1960s to make room for large demonstrations in what became Green Square. A Libyan blog instead says it was demolished in the late 1960s, before the coup.
today: Gone. A 2018 lecture on its history was held at Dar Hassan al-Faqih in Tripoli.
uncertain: Demolition date (late 1960s vs after 1969) and architect are not settled. No coordinates are given.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: Tripoli's lost elegance of Miramare Theatre

name: Lungomare Conte Volpi (the Corniche)
summary: The Italian-built waterfront boulevard along the harbour, laid out under governor Giuseppe Volpi.
history: Giuseppe Volpi governed Tripolitania from 1921 to 1925 and hired architect Armando Brasini to lead its renovation, including the waterfront boulevard. Wikipedia's timeline dates the Lungomare Conte Volpi to 1924. A Columbia University lantern-slide record shows it as "Il Lungomare Conte Volpi" in the early 20th century. The promenade was once considered among the most beautiful on the Mediterranean.
era: In the 1970s a road expansion project filled in a long stretch of the sea, so the Corniche has no sea in front of it; the Red Castle also lost its sea frontage and Saraya Lake formed.
uncertain: The extent of the original waterfront is not mapped here, so no point is given. Brasini's role is stated in a blog.

name: Gazelle Fountain (Gazelle and the Beauty)
summary: A bronze Italian fountain of a seated woman and a gazelle on the Corniche, a symbol of Tripoli.
history: Designed by the Italian sculptor Angiolo Vannetti in 1932, originally named "Sorgente di Vita" (Source of Life). It shows a nude woman on a rock embracing a gazelle, set in water, facing the sea. Historian David Rifkind reads the woman as Italy and the gazelle as Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, united in 1934. Vannetti said the work expressed the city, the gazelle the desert and the woman the sea.
era: Gaddafi spared it, along with two harbour columns topped by Romulus and Remus, even while removing other Italian monuments. The 1970s road works filled in the sea in front of it.
today: Cleaned in 2012; wrapped in blue cloth in 2012, hit by an RPG in 2013, and removed in 2014. In February 2021 a plain fountain replaced it.
uncertain: The coordinates are OpenStreetMap's "Statue Belle and Spinner" point, a mislabelled English name for the gazelle statue. Where the statue was kept after 2014 is not stated.

name: Tripoli International Fair
summary: The oldest trade fair in Africa, founded by the Italian colonial government.
history: Founded by the Italian government in 1927 and promoted alongside the Tripoli Grand Prix to showcase Italian Libya. In the 1930s it was one of the main international fairs of the colonial world; the 1934 fair became known for a first air trip across an oasis of the Libyan Sahara, commemorated by an Italian stamp. The most notable structure is a symbolic monument at the entrance, the Pavilion of the Governorate of Rome, by the Egyptian-born Italian architect Alessandro Limongelli. After World War II the fair reopened on a much smaller scale.
today: The 2008 edition ran 2-12 April and in 2010 over 1,000 participants from 29 countries took part.
uncertain: The fairground location, its Gaddafi-era role, and whether the pavilion survives were not found, so no coordinates.

name: Italian Cemetery and Memorial (Hammangi)
summary: The large Italian municipal Christian cemetery and war memorial in the Hammangi/Mansura area, next to the British war cemetery.
history: The Italian municipal Christian cemetery holds the Hammangi memorial, which housed Italian Second World War dead brought to Tripoli under King Idris. The cemetery once held about 15,000 bodies across 12 hectares. The Tripoli War Cemetery is reached through its gate. A separate OpenStreetMap node labelled the "Christian cemetery" lies close by.
era: After the 1970 coup, thousands of remains, including those of Italo Balbo, were repatriated to Italy. The cemetery was left without guards or staff; in 2004 the president of the Italian returnees' association said dogs were among the graves. Ten hectares were returned to the Tripoli municipality, and a first restoration was finished in 2009.
today: After 2011 vandals looted copper and damaged mosaics. A restoration costing about EUR 350,000, designed by Renato Proietti, started in 2019, and the memorial reopened on 7 October 2020 with a Mass. A rocket hit the adjacent British cemetery on 31 May 2020 and grazed the memorial.
uncertain: The cemetery's founding year is not given. Coordinates are OpenStreetMap's "Italian cemetery" area.

sources.t: Italian Foreign Ministry: Hammangi Italian memorial restored

name: Tripoli War Cemetery (Commonwealth)
summary: The Commonwealth war graves cemetery for the Second World War, entered through the old Italian cemetery.
history: Montgomery's Eighth Army captured Tripoli on 23 January 1943, after which the city became a hospital centre. Burials came almost entirely from hospitals, including No. 2, No. 48 and No. 133 General Hospitals from March 1943 and No. 89 General Hospital from April 1944. There are 1,369 Commonwealth Second World War burials, 133 of them unidentified, plus 19 non-Commonwealth and 7 non-war-service burials. It lies in the Mansura district, about 2.5 km west of the centre, off the west end of Sharia Jamahuriya.
today: The Commission planned a renovation of several Libyan cemeteries because the climate has eroded headstones. A rocket fell on the adjacent British cemetery on 31 May 2020.
uncertain: The founding date is not given. The Gaddafi-era upkeep is not documented in the sources opened. Coordinates are from the ww2cemeteries page.

sources.t: Italian Foreign Ministry: Hammangi Italian memorial restored

name: Janzur (Zanzur) and Italian Giorgimpopoli
summary: A coastal town west of Tripoli, site of the 1912 battles and of an Italian-period settlement.
history: First settled in the 6th century BC. It was a district of the Ottoman sanjak of Tripoli; in 1862 it was split into Janzour and Al-Aziziya. On 6 March 1912 Italian airships bombed Turkish troops and Libyan fighters camped at Janzour, the first use of airships in war, according to a New York Times report of 8 March. A Jewish community lived there until the end of World War II, when a local synagogue was burned and Jews were killed in the November 1945 pogrom. Under the Kingdom it belonged to the Tripoli governorate.
era: It became a municipality in 1983 and was later reassigned between districts: Tripoli in 1995, Zawia in 1998 and Al-Jafara in 2001. It now hosts the Libyan Academy and some faculties of the University of Tripoli.
uncertain: The name Giorgimpopoli, mentioned in the request, is not in the sources opened, so the link is not confirmed. Coordinates are the Wikipedia town centre.

name: Italian colonist villages around Tripoli
summary: Planned agricultural settlements founded for Italian farming families, some of them near Tripoli.
history: Italian colonists concentrated in the farmland around Tripoli. In 1938 Italy founded 26 agricultural villages for about 20,000 colonists, including Gioda, Crispi, Olivetti and Breviglieri. Settlers had to come from large families, pass medical and background checks, and have a household head in the Fascist party. The Tripoli area held the largest Italian community in the colony: 47,400 Italians among 113,212 residents in 1939. In January 1939 the coastal areas became part of metropolitan Italy.
era: In 1970 Gaddafi ordered the expulsion of about 20,000 remaining Italians and nationalised Italian companies. Their property was confiscated, valued at about 3 billion euros today. The Italian population had fallen to about 1,500 by 1986.
uncertain: The exact locations of the villages near Tripoli were not given in sources opened, so no coordinates. Wikipedia says most of the farming villages were in Cyrenaica. The internment camps of the 1930s were in Cyrenaica, not Tripoli, so none are listed here.

name: Mellaha Air Base / Wheelus Air Base / Okba Ben Nafi / Mitiga
ar: قاعدة عقبة بن نافع الجوية / معيتيقة
summary: The Italian airfield that became the huge US Wheelus Air Base and later Tripoli's Mitiga airport.
history: The Italian Air Force built it in 1923 as Mellaha Air Base; the Luftwaffe used it in the North African campaign. The British Eighth Army captured it in January 1943 and US forces used it that month. It became Wheelus Army Air Field on 17 May 1945, named for Lt Richard Wheelus, closed in 1947 and reopened as Wheelus Air Base on 1 June 1948. A 1954 agreement ran to 1971. Its radio station began in 1954 and its TV station on 15 September 1956 was among the first in the Arab world. In 1967-68 King Idris planned to close foreign bases, the largest being Wheelus.
era: Handed to Libya on 11 June 1970 (evacuation completed March 1970 by another count) and renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base, it housed the air force headquarters and training, with Soviet aircraft and personnel. The US bombed it on 16 April 1986. In 1995 it became a civilian airport called Mitiga.
today: Since 2018 it has been Tripoli's only international airport; it closed on 8 April 2019 after airstrikes and flights resumed in May 2021.
uncertain: Handover date varies between sources (March vs 11 June 1970). Coordinates are Wikipedia's 32°53'42"N 13°16'49"E and give the airfield centre only.

sources.t: Libyan Heritage House: Wheelus radio and TV station

name: Castel Benito Airfield (Tripoli Idris Airport)
summary: The Italian airfield south of Tripoli that became King Idris's international airport and Tripoli International Airport.
history: A Regia Aeronautica airfield built in 1934 on the southern outskirts of Italian Tripoli. In 1938 Governor Italo Balbo expanded it into a civilian international airport for Ala Littoria, with routes to Rome, Tunis and Malta. The British Eighth Army captured it in January 1943, after Allied raids had destroyed it; three days later a BOAC Lockheed 14 landed there. The Royal Engineers built three runways that year. After independence in 1951 it was renamed Idris el Awal (Idris I) and was the only thing named after the king.
era: After the 1969 revolution it was renamed Tripoli International Airport. A new 09/27 runway started in 1966 was completed later, and a new terminal opened on 28 July 1978. Wikipedia does not name Gaddafi in its account of the airport.
today: Fighting from 14 July to 23 August 2014 destroyed at least 90 percent of its facilities and 20 aircraft; passenger flights moved to Mitiga.
uncertain: Whether the Castel Benito name predates 1934 is unknown. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia infobox.

name: Mellaha Lake Grand Prix Circuit
summary: A fast 13 km road circuit around Mellaha Lake and airfield, home of the Tripoli Grand Prix.
history: The Grand Prix was held 14 times from 1925 to 1940, and from 1933 on the Mellaha Lake circuit, 13.14 km long, in a salt basin between Tripoli, Suq al Jum'ah and Tajura. A grandstand held up to 10,000, and a white concrete tower opposite it was the track's most distinctive feature. The race was tied to the state lottery, sold in 12-lire tickets from October 1932 with prizes of up to 3 million lire. The last race was on 12 May 1940, won by Giuseppe Farina. The airfield was built inside the circuit.
uncertain: A story of a fixed 1933 race is considered a probable myth. What remains of the grandstand and tower is not stated. Coordinates are Wikipedia's approximate circuit centre.

name: Tripoli Central Station and the Tripoli-Tajura line
summary: The Italian-built station that began three narrow-gauge lines, including a 21 km line east to Tajura.
history: Tripoli Central was the start of three Italian lines: Tripoli-Zuara (118 km), Tripoli-Garian (90 km) and Tripoli-Tagiura (21 km, ten stations). They used 950 mm gauge, and Gurgi and Gargaresc were the first two stops on the Zuara and Garian lines. Italy built nearly 400 km of railway in Libya and none after 1926. After the 1911 Ain Zara battle the Italians built a line linking that oasis to Tripoli. A Tripoli-Benghazi line begun in 1941 was never finished.
today: Wikipedia lists Tripoli Central station among the Italian-era buildings later demolished, without a date.
uncertain: Opening years for each line, the tramway named in the request, and the station site are not documented in the sources opened; no coordinates are given.

name: Shar al-Shatt (Sciara Sciat) battlefield
summary: The eastern oasis district of Tripoli where Ottoman and Arab forces attacked the Italians on 23-26 October 1911.
history: The battle took place 23-26 October 1911 on the outskirts of Tripoli. Ottoman and Arab forces attacked the thinly fortified eastern sector, held by the 11th Bersaglieri, firing from the oasis and houses. The 4th Company barricaded itself in a cemetery and surrendered; about 290 surrendered soldiers were killed. Italian official losses were 503 dead and 158 wounded. The Italians retook the area on the evening of 23 October. Harsh reprisals followed on 24 October, and one account says thousands of civilians died and a mosque with 100 refugees inside was burned.
uncertain: Casualty figures vary widely between and within sources. Wikipedia's coordinates give the battle area only, not a specific site. A Bersaglieri monument at Porta Pia in Rome commemorates it.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Battle and massacre at Shar al-Shatt

name: Ain Zara battlefield and memorial
summary: The oasis south-east of Tripoli where the Italians won the battle of 4 December 1911.
history: On 4 December 1911 about 12,000 Italians in three columns attacked about 8,000 Ottoman and Arab troops holding a well-fortified position with eight Krupp guns, about 8 km south of Tripoli. The Ottoman side withdrew in the afternoon and left its guns. Italian losses were 17 killed and 171 wounded, including Colonel Giovanni Pastorelli. The Italians then fortified the oasis and built a railway linking it to Tripoli. On 28 January 1912 about 4,000 Ottoman and Arab fighters tried to retake it and were repelled.
uncertain: The point is the OpenStreetMap "Memorial Ain Zara" node rather than the exact field. Casualty figures for the opposing forces are rough. Troops digging trenches found a Roman mosaic, probably from Oea, which was sent to Italy.

sources.t: OpenStreetMap node 4127652191 (Memorial Ain Zara) (project extract landmarks.json)

name: Monument to the Battle of Hani
summary: A memorial in the Hani area east of Tripoli commemorating the 1911 fighting.
history: OpenStreetMap maps two memorial points here, "Monument to the Battle of Hani" and "The memorial of the HANI battle". The Hani area lies in the eastern oasis belt, about 1.5 km south-east of the coordinates Wikipedia gives for the Shar al-Shatt fighting of October 1911. The battle ran 23-26 October 1911; Ottoman and Arab forces attacked from the oasis and Italian reprisals followed.
uncertain: None of the pages opened name Hani as the Libyan name for the Shar al-Shatt battle, so that link is an inference. The memorial's date, builder and the year of the battle it marks are unknown.

name: Fort Hamidiye and Fort Sultaniye (1911 landing)
summary: The two Ottoman harbour forts shelled by the Italian fleet on 3-4 October 1911.
history: Starting at 15:30 on 3 October 1911 an Italian squadron fired on Forts Hamidiye and Sultaniye from about 9,500 m, then closer, leaving the forts badly damaged; the Ottoman gunboat Seyyad and the steamer Derna were scuttled. Captain Umberto Cagni's naval landing force went ashore on 5 October, took Fort Sultaniye and raised the Italian flag at noon, while sappers took Fort Hamidiye. By 16:30 troops reached the marketplace. Italian strength in the city rose to about 35,000 by 11 October.
uncertain: Neither fort was matched to a surviving building or to an OpenStreetMap feature; no coordinates are given. The Wikipedia battle page shows the city centre only.

name: Bab al-Azizia (barracks and Gaddafi compound)
summary: A large military compound south of the centre: Italian barracks, rebuilt under King Idris, then Gaddafi's fortified headquarters until 2011.
history: The site was an Italian army base before and during World War II. British forces occupied the barracks in December 1945, and King Idris rebuilt the compound. Al-Aziziya itself was created in 1862 as a sub-district of Janzour. The sources opened do not describe the site in the Ottoman period or the 1911 fighting.
era: Gaddafi made it his main base. In the 1980s it was reinforced and expanded by foreign contractors, with three concrete walls, tunnels, a mosque, a pool and a residence. A coup attempt there on 8 May 1984 failed. The US bombed it on 15 April 1986; Gaddafi later put up a monument of a fist crushing a US aircraft.
today: Rebels captured it on 23 August 2011. Demolition of the outer walls began in October 2011. By February 2012 many buildings were rubble, with some families living in makeshift homes. Proposals to turn it into a park were not finalised.
uncertain: Whether the Azizia name pre-dates the Italian base is unclear. Coordinates are from Wikipedia's infobox.

name: University of Libya, Tripoli faculties (1957)
summary: The Tripoli branch of the first Libyan university, which began with a Faculty of Science.
history: The University of Libya began in 1957 and its Tripoli branch started with the Faculty of Science, one of the first practical colleges in the country. The Faculty of Agriculture was added in 1966. After the 1969 coup the Tripoli and Benghazi campuses were subject to a crackdown.
era: A college of petroleum and minerals was added in 1972. In 1973 the University of Libya split into Tripoli and Benghazi universities, and in 1976 Tripoli was renamed Al Fateh University after student unrest that April. Political activity was heavily restricted from the early 1970s; by the late 1970s opponents could be arrested. The medical school was ordered to admit about 2,000 students against a capacity of roughly 150.
today: Renamed University of Tripoli in 2012. The present main campus is in south-east Tripoli at about 32.856 N, 13.221 E.
uncertain: The original 1957 site of the Faculty of Science is not stated, so no coordinates are given. The campus coordinates (32°51'21"N 13°13'17"E) are the later university, not necessarily the 1957 building.

name: Port of Tripoli
summary: The country's main seaport, a Roman harbour that Italy rebuilt in the late 1920s.
history: In Roman times the port of Oea was one of the main ports of the African Mediterranean coast; it declined in the Middle Ages and revived under Ottoman rule. Italian authorities built the port that exists today in the late 1920s and added a seaplane facility in the 1930s. World War II badly damaged it. The British governed it until independence in 1951. Tripoli's harbour fortifications, Forts Hamidiye and Sultaniye, were shelled on 3-4 October 1911.
era: In the 1970s it was greatly expanded with many cargo terminals, a yacht club and a fishing wharf. Congestion was long-standing, with average waits to unload reaching 24 days in 1977. Dry cargo capacity rose from 10.5 million tons in 1976 to 13.7 million tons in 1980. It was run by the Socialist Ports Company.
today: A harbour of about 300 hectares with breakwaters of 2,000 m and 700 m. Coordinates are from Wikipedia. A lighthouse was not documented in the sources opened.
uncertain: No Tripoli lighthouse was found in sources opened. The percent of Italian-era works remaining is unknown.

name: 1945 anti-Jewish riots in Tripoli (sites)
summary: The 5-7 November 1945 riots under British military administration, in which synagogues and Jewish homes in Tripoli were attacked.
history: The riots ran from 5 to 7 November 1945 in Tripolitania, then under British occupation, after a wave of rioting on 2 November in Aleppo and Cairo. In Tripoli, 38 people were killed; the toll across the region was over 140, including 36 children. Rioters looted nearly all of Tripoli's synagogues and destroyed five, and plundered over 1,000 Jewish homes and businesses. About 4,000 Jews were left homeless. The British were criticised for responding slowly; at least 550 Muslims were arrested and tried in British military courts.
uncertain: Which streets and synagogues in Tripoli were hit is not named in the sources opened, so no coordinates are given. The page's town totals add to 135 not "more than 140". Villages such as Amrus (40 killed), Zanzur (34), Tajura (7) and Zawia (13) were also hit. Further riots in June 1948 killed 12.

sources.t: Wikipedia: History of the Jews in Libya

name: 1967 Six-Day War riots in Tripoli
summary: The June 1967 anti-Jewish and anti-Western riots that triggered the departure of most of the remaining Jewish community.
history: On 15 June 1967 Libyan youths held violent demonstrations backing the Arab states at war with Israel, which led to the deaths of many Jews and the destruction of US and British property. Wikipedia says the unrest included attacks on US and British embassies and oil company offices. After the war, anti-Jewish violence killed 18. King Idris allowed Jews to leave temporarily, and the Italian Navy helped evacuate over 6,000 of them to Rome within a month. About 7,000 remaining Jews were evacuated overall, according to another page.
uncertain: The pages opened do not say which of these attacks were in Tripoli, or name particular buildings. Casualty figures differ. No coordinates are given.

sources.t: Wikipedia: History of the Jews in Libya

name: 1 September 1969 coup in Tripoli (radio station and barracks)
summary: The overnight coup that ended the monarchy; in Tripoli, officers seized the radio station, barracks, anti-aircraft batteries and airports.
history: On 1 September 1969 Free Officers under Gaddafi staged a coup while King Idris was in Turkey for treatment, launching in Benghazi and finishing within two hours. In Tripoli, Khweldi Hameidi captured the radio station, Umar Muhayshi took over the barracks, and Abdessalam Jalloud seized the anti-aircraft batteries. The officers also occupied airports, police depots and government offices. Hameidi was sent to arrest Crown Prince Hasan ar-Rida and make him renounce his claim. Military control of Tripoli was established within a few days.
era: Gaddafi ended the monarchy and proclaimed a republic. The queen's private secretary was placed under house probation by officers led by Omar Almheishi and later released after negotiations, by her own account. Idris went into exile in Egypt and was sentenced to death in absentia in 1971.
uncertain: The pages opened give no addresses for the radio station or barracks, and the Wheelus connection is not documented. A memoir by the queen's secretary is a personal account. No coordinates are given.

sources.t: Libyan Wanderer: Queen Fatima's private secretary, 1968-69
